“The Boys Of Tandragee” ~ lyrics

Good luck to all here now barring the cat that sits in the corner there smelling a rat
Ah whisht you philandering girls and behave and saving your presence, I’ll chant you a stave
I come from a land where the praties grow big and the girls neat and handy can dance a fine jig
And the boys they would charm your heart for to see they’re wonderful fellas round Tandragee

Chorus: So here’s to the boys who are happy and gay
Singing and dancing and tearing away
Rollicksome, frollicksome, frisky and free
We’re the rollicking boys around Tandragee

No doubt you have heard of Killarney I’m sure and sweet Inishowen for the drop of the pure
Dublin’s the place for the Strawberry Beds and Donnybrook Fair for the cracking of heads
Did you e’re see an Irishman dancing poltog, how he faces his partner and turns up his brogue
He shakes at the buckle and bends at the knee, they’re wonderfull dancers round Tandragee

Chorus

The oul’ jaunting car is the elegant joult, and Derry’s the place that is famed for the hoult
Among the green bushes that grow in Tyrone, and the County Fermanagh for muscle and bone
But for feasting and blarney and fun at the fair there’s none to compare with the Rakes of Kildare
Green Erin’s my country, the gem of the sea, but the gem of oul Ireland is Tandragee

Chorus

Now where is the man either Christian or Turk could equal the bold Robert Emmet or Burke
Where is the lawyer could speak up like Dan, there’s devil another, bad luck to the one
And where is the singer could sing like Tom Moore, whose melodies charm every care from your door
We’ll beat them all yet boys, and that you will see, sure we’re rearing fine fellas round Tandragee

Chorus

Re: The Rollicking Boys Of Tandragee

Paddy Tunney said he learned it from his Uncle Mick (Michael) Gallagher. It was recorded by the Tunney family in 1952, when Colum was less than a year old. Precocious wean! A Sean Nos teacher told us that it was written in the 1800s to poke fun at the very straight-laced (at the time bordering on Puritanical, according to him) citizenry of Tanderagee (now called Tandragee). Its lyrics and especially the chorus were therefore intended to be entirely satirical, although the tune has such a great drive and dynamic that it will always be performed with joy, and of course it’s been so long that probably there *are* many fine dancers ’round Tandragee these days!

Hi Mark - that makes a lot of sense - I don’t think there’s any issue with the first setting, I just wanted to make that comment so anyone reading it would get an insight into Finbarr’s style. It’s funny, because if you’re used to playing C#/D box, then you would need to mentally transpose to get it up where Finbarr played it, whereas if you’re used to playing B/C, you just pick up a different box. Technically it’s exactly the same thing (it is, after all, the same fingering), it’s just the mental aspect behind it that’s different.

↳ Posted by Nico on May 3rd, 2021.

Re: The Rollicking Boys Of Tandragee

Hi Nico,
Everything you wrote is right, but, of course, there’s more to what Finbarr did than just
playing B/C fingering on C#/D box. His choice of notes, ornamentation, timing, etc… is unlike anyone else.
This tune, The Boys of Tandaragee, is usually played in E minor, so the concept of putting it into mixolydian
mode (whether Dmix or Emix) is Finbarr’s own idea.
(It seems fairly common to his versions of tunes that he likes the thirds to be major rather than minor,
at least some of the time.)
So it’s not like people would think “Oh, that’s the usual D version played up a step”. Instead they think
“Wow! The usual version reimagined to use G#s, octave jumps, and cool variations!”

↳ Posted by brianbeag on May 17th, 2022.

Re: The Rollicking Boys Of Tandragee

Did you mean Finbarr Dwyer? There’s no link to a Richie Dwyer (or to “Ricard”) recording here…

In any case as already mentioned, the audio is a half step higher, either because he’s playing a D/D# box or because the audio is incorrectly sharp. The convention, long established, is to write out music as if for a concert pitch instrument, despite the absolute pitch. So if I were to play an Eb flute, or a set of B uilleann pipes, or a box that’s a half-step higher than normal, I would write the music out as if it was a normal D flute, D pipes, or regular box. The issue here is that there are actually two “normal” pitches of button box, B/C and C#/D, both thought of as concert pitch. Finbarr Dwyer was essentially a B/C box player who would play a C#/D or D/D# box as if it were a B/C box (there’s more nuance described above, of course), but ultimately the convention would be to transcribe the music as if it were a concert pitch box, so either Emix or Dmix depending on whether you’re thinking of B/C or C#/D as the concert pitch box in question.

I don’t agree that it’s dorian because the 3rds are sharp, although he does avoid them often.
